analysis.one_liner: Lets drug companies win extra monopoly years on patents whose FDA review took over five years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let drug companies extend already-extended patents for up to five more years, never got a vote after a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in August 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new way for drug companies to get more years added to patents on medicines whose FDA approval took longer than five years, even if those patents had already been extended once. During the extra years, generic copies could not be approved, so the monopoly on the drug would last longer. To soften the blow, companies that had already invested in making generic versions would get fixed payments of up to a few million dollars, and the bill would limit some of the patents brand companies could use to block generic applications.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug companies holding patents on medicines whose FDA review took more than five years would gain up to five extra years of exclusive sales — years in which no generic competitor could be approved. Companies that had invested in developing generic versions would receive fixed compensation payments, and generic applicants would face somewhat easier certification rules.

how_it_helps.text: It lets owners of drug patents that were already extended once (subject to a two-year cap) apply for additional restoration of up to five years if the FDA review took over 60 months, the owner showed due diligence, and the grant was not found to hurt the public interest [S2][S3].
During the review, the Patent Office could extend an expiring patent by up to one year, and a certificate of restoration would take effect immediately upon issuance [S3].

It offsets the added delay for generic makers by (a) paying $2 million to any generic applicant already on file and $1 million to Type II Drug Master File holders, (b) limiting which patents a generic must certify against (only those claiming the active ingredient), and (c) adding a 45-day window for the brand to sue over a restored patent, after which the generic's exclusivity clock could run [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients, insurers, and government health programs, who would keep paying brand-name prices for drugs whose patents were extended, for up to five additional years per drug.

drawbacks.text: The core effect is to lengthen drug monopolies: restored patents block generic competition for up to five more years, which means patients and insurers pay brand-name prices longer, and the bill's own public-interest test acknowledges the tension with 'the availability of innovative drugs at competitive prices' [S2][S3].

The compensation for generic companies that had already invested in copying the drug — $2 million per applicant, $1 million per file holder, capped at $10 million and $5 million per patent owner — is a small, fixed payment set by statute, not a market-based measure of what those firms or patients lose from delayed generic entry [S3].

Applications had to be filed within 90 days of enactment, and the Commissioner's decision could be appealed only to the specialized Federal Circuit, concentrating review of these monopoly extensions in a single patent-friendly court [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gave brand-name drug companies a second chance at monopoly extension on patents already extended once, in exchange for capped, relatively small payouts to generic makers and limits on using method-of-use patents to block generics. The cost fell on consumers, who would pay brand prices longer; the compensation caps were too small to offset that. The generic-blocking limits were a genuine concession, but the core effect was a transfer from patients to patent holders.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got one hearing in August 1999, and then sat there until the Congress ended without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Torricelli introduced the bill on May 27, 1999, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1][S5].
Ten senators signed on as cosponsors, eight Republicans and two Democrats [S4].
The Judiciary Committee held a hearing on the bill on August 4, 1999 (printed as S.Hrg. 106-772), but no markup or vote followed [S5].
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill died in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Generic drug makers and everyone who buys prescription drugs are better off that the patent extensions never happened; the bill's death preserved the existing limits on drug monopolies.

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1][S3].

for.name: 8 of 10 cosponsors (Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan cover [S4].

for.name: Senate Committee on the Judiciary
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on August 4, 1999, but took the bill no further [S5].

against.name: Generic drug industry
against.what_they_did: The generic drug industry broadly opposed legislation extending brand-name drug patents, since each extra monopoly year blocks generic approval and sales; this bill's compensation payments (capped at $10 million per patent owner) were small relative to what a delayed generic launch loses.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with 8 of his 10 cosponsors Republican — so the bill's failure was not a party-line defeat but a matter of the committee never acting on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would give their longest-reviewed, already-extended drug patents up to five more years of monopoly pricing, with a small, capped payout to generic challengers as the only cost. Generic entry would be delayed, keeping revenue flowing on old drugs.

They would face extra years of blocked approvals on restored patents, but would receive statutory compensation ($2 million per applicant, capped) and would only have to certify against patents claiming the active ingredient, making some challenges easier.

industries.industry: Consumers and payers of prescription drugs
industries.note: Extended monopolies mean longer periods without generic competition, which is when prices are highest. Ordinary people would pay more for prescription drugs for longer.
